newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia rejects call to end Cambodian aid.
newsitem.headline: Australia rejects call to end Cambodian aid.

text.p: Australia on Wednesday rejected Cambodian opposition calls to end aid to the southeast Asian nation, but renewed its warning to Cambodian strongman Hun Sen to hold fair elections and honour 1991 peace accords.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer told opposition leader Sam Rainsy that cutting Australia's A$32 million (US$24 million) annual aid programme would only hurt Cambodia's poor.
"If we cut our aid programme as Mr Rainsy has suggested, we would deny food, water and health care to thousands of poor Cambodians," Downer said in a statement after talks with Sam Rainsy.

"I stressed, however, that the continuation of our aid programme is absolutely conditional on the performance of the Cambodian government in living up to the commitments it has made in regard to human rights, free and fair elections and respect for the principles on the Paris peace accords."
Sam Rainsy, an outspoken former finance minister in Cambodia's ruling coalition, now heads an anti-Hun Sen coalition and is in Australia to lobby for support from Canberra and expatriate Khmers.

"I think any assistance provided to or through the Phnom Penh authorities must be suspended until the legal government is reinstated ... and there are some assurances that free and fair elections will be held as scheduled next May," the Khmer Nation Party chief told Reuters on Tuesday.
"As a former finance minister, I can tell you how dependent any (Cambodian) administration is on international assistance, so Hun Sen cannot afford to avoid free and fair elections."
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen seized power with military backing last month, ousting his coalition partner and First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.
Cambodia's parliament last week voted to replace Ranariddh with Foreign Minister Ung Huot, a member of the prince's party, in a move condemned by opposition politicians.
